item.title: 87% of the Anthropic power will come from gas and 11% from coal in 2028 (198 pts)
item.description:
URL: https://betterdatacenterproject.com/2026/11/16/how-ai-is-powered-a-breakdown-of-byop-and-grid-power/, See on Hacker News

In The AI Gas Rush: Risks and Implications of “Bring Your Own Power”, we dug into how data centers are increasingly securing their own dedicated primary power generation rather than relying solely on utilities to procure power (“BYOP”). We identified 177 GW of planned BYOP gas capacity—enough to power 65% of all US homes. Conversely, we found renewables are much less common than gas for BYOP: we estimate that for current proposals, less than 20% of energy generation will come from renewable sources by 2032.

But BYOP projects aren’t the only new fossil sources that are coming online to meet the skyrocketing energy demands of AI data centers. Another 200 GW of new fossil power plants is being built on the grid to meet growing demand, due in large part to data centers.1

As a case study of how the AI buildout is driving both new BYOP and grid fossil infrastructure, we analyzed the compute commitments of a single company: Anthropic.

Map of Anthropic’s data centers and associated power plants. See our full dataset for details of each site.

Finding 1: Anthropic has made no direct commitments to renewable energy in the U.S. Though Anthropic has stated “We’re also working to broaden our energy mix with geothermal, wind, solar, and emerging technologies”, its only publicly disclosed commitments, contract, or investments in renewable power are in Norway and Canada (as of November 2026). In contrast, Anthropic is directly procuring fossil power equipment—it recently “bought commitments for 1.7 gigawatts of heavy-duty [gas] generators for $3.4bn”.

Finding 2: Anthropic’s currently contracted data centers in the U.S. will be overwhelmingly powered by fossil fuels in the near term. By considering on-site gas and the grid power plants which are likely to meet Anthropic’s added load (i.e. marginal generators), we estimate about 87% of the company’s power will come from gas and 11% from coal in 2028. As of October 2026, Anthropic has contracted 15 GW of compute; of this, about 5.9–9.6 GW is contracted to specific data center sites. For a sense of scale, 9.6 GW could power about 7 million homes or cover 18% of the peak power demand of California—the world’s 4th largest economy.

This demand will be met with a mix of new on-site gas, new grid gas, and existing grid gas, coal, and nuclear. In the short term, no grid renewables are attributed to Anthropic’s power use, because—without commitments to new renewable capacity—new load on the grid will be met by dispatchable, marginal fossil resources.2 For more details, see our full dataset and our methodology below.

Finding 3: Total CO2 emissions from Anthropic’s power use at these sites could reach 17–38 million MtCO2e per year in 2028, when this capacity is expected to be online. This range reflects uncertainty in Anthropic’s average power use, due to factors such as cooling needs and average utilization (see methodology below). In our mid-case, Anthropic will emit 32 million MtCO2e in 2028. These totals will continue to grow—possibly doubling by 2030, as some analysts expect Anthropic to secure 30 GW by 2030.

To put these figures in context, Anthropic’s CO2 emissions from power use in 2028:

  • could exceed the emissions of all of California’s power generation (31.1 MMtCO2e in 2024, not including imports).
  • could exceed Meta, Microsoft, and Google’s combined Scope 2 emissions from 2025 (their location-based emissions, before renewable energy offsets, were 5.9 million, 12 million and 15 million MtCO2e, respectively)3
  • would represent a 16–36% increase over 2024 levels of the entire U.S. data center sector (105 MMtCO2e).
  • would increase the entire U.S.’s power sector emissions (1,485 MMtCO2e in 2025) by 1.1–2.5%.

Finding 4: Anthropic’s data centers are sited in areas where the grid mainly uses coal and gas. We estimate the average carbon intensity of Anthropic’s power to be 1,033–1,076 lb CO2e/MWh, 35% higher than the U.S. grid average (767 lb CO2e/MWh).4

Finding 5: 80% of on-site power uses inefficient simple cycle turbines and engines. About 25% (2.5 GW) of Anthropic’s contracted power will come from on-site, behind-the-meter gas. 80% of this on-site capacity consists of inefficient simple cycle turbines and engines, which emit more pollution per unit of electricity than modern combined cycle plants (see our report for more details on the types of power generation being used for on-site gas).

Finding 6: Based on EPA’s nationally-averaged benefit-per-ton estimates, air pollution from Anthropic’s on-site and grid power use could cause $2–3 billion in annual health damages, with total emissions of over 13,000 tons per year (tpy) of nitrogen oxides (NOx) and 2,000 tpy of fine particulate matter (PM2.5).

In October 2026, Anthropic outlined its “approach to responsible data center development”, stating: “We follow the air permitting process everywhere we operate and require the same of the plants powering our data centers. Those plants must also use emissions control technology, including selective catalytic reduction [SCR].” However, Anthropic has used compute capacity at SpaceX’s Colossus 2 facility since May 2026, which still receives most of its power from temporary, unpermitted turbines, the majority of which are not equipped with SCR. Anthropic will use as much as 600 MW of power from Colossus 2 by the end of 2026 (see methodology below).

Anthropic has also contracted 460 MW (and is in talks for up to 920 MW) of power from Nscale’s Monarch Compute Campus in Mason, West Virginia. This facility will be powered by inefficient reciprocating engines which have significant formaldehyde and hazardous air pollutant (HAP) emissions compared to conventional gas power plants.

For more, see our full dataset on Anthropic’s compute and our report on BYOP.

Methodology

We gathered details about Anthropic’s data center commitments from Epoch AI’s tracker, Anthropic’s announcements and filings, announcements and filings from partners (including Amazon and SpaceX), and reporting from The Information, Semafor, and others.

We first identified the source for each data center’s power. For projects with on-site gas (Monarch, Nexus, Colossus 2) or new grid gas (including indirectly contracted projects such as the Schahfer expansion for the AWS New Carlisle site and Entergy Mississippi’s gas plants for AWS’s Madison and Ridgeland facilities) we used emissions factors from permits where available, or permit values from comparable facilities. For grid-connected facilities without associated new generation capacity, we assume these sites will be powered by marginal, dispatchable grid capacity. We used EPA’s AVERT tool to model which power plants would meet the new incremental load from Anthropic’s facilities based on each site’s expected power use and region. AVERT uses historical EPA data for these power plants to model the expected short-run marginal emissions rate of CO2 and criteria pollutants (NOx, PM2.5, etc.). We use AVERT because we are interested in the short-term impacts from new data centers coming online in the next several years.

To calculate the amount of power used by each site, and in turn the total quantity of air pollutant emissions, we assumed power usage effectiveness (PUE) ranges from 1.1–1.2 for all sites (typical values for hyperscale data centers are between 1.05–1.3), and power utilization ranges from 60–80%. See LBNL’s 2024 Data Center Energy Usage report for more details about how these parameters vary in typical hyperscale data centers. For our mid-case, we assumed a PUE of 1.15, a power utilization of 70%, and that all 9.6 GW of identified compute capacity is online in 2028.

How much capacity is Anthropic leasing from xAI?

Anthropic’s initial announcement on May 6, 2026 stated the agreement with SpaceX provided 300 MW of compute (220,000 GPUs). From SpaceX’s revised June S-1A, this deal expanded to ~$1.25B/month for 325,000 NVIDIA GPUs,5 with an implied IT power of ~490 MW. Based on Anthropic’s October 2026 S-1, this deal has further expanded to $3.1B/month.6 It’s unlikely that the increase in $/month will result in a proportional (2.5x) increase in compute capacity, since a June 2026 deal between Google and SpaceX had a much higher cost (~$11.5/GPU-hr vs ~$5/GPU-hr). As a rough estimate, the scaled deal likely corresponds to an additional ~200,000 GPUs, with a total power of ~400 MW (uncertainty is probably ±25% for each).7

  1. Data centers are driving 50–75% of demand growth, according to IEA and McKinsey. ↩︎
  2. For more discussion, see for example: Fassette, Camille. “The emissions risks of AI data center buildout.” WattTime. February, 2025; EPRI. “Powering Data Centers: U.S. Energy System and Emissions Impacts of Growing Loads.” October, 2024. ↩︎
  3. Note: Anthropic’s emissions from power use will likely be classified as a mix of Scope 2 and Scope 3 emissions, depending on if they own the GPUs. For facilities they are leasing space in, the emissions will likely be accounted for as Scope 2 emissions for the owner/operator (e.g. Amazon for Project Rainier or SpaceX for Colossus). It should also be noted that the emissions of Microsoft, Google, and Meta are expected to grow as well, so the comparison between their 2025 emissions and Anthropic’s 2028 emissions is not meant to suggest that Anthropic will be the largest emitter among the tech companies. ↩︎
  4. This average is based on AVERT’s marginal emissions for grid-connected units without new dedicated capacity. Using the average (non-marginal) carbon intensity for each eGRID subregion would give a carbon intensity of 839 lb CO2/MWh. However, marginal emissions are more representative of the near-term impacts of Anthropic’s added load to the grid. ↩︎
  5. Pg. 13: “For example, in May 2026, we entered into Cloud Services Agreements with Anthropic PBC (“Anthropic”), an AI research and development public benefit corporation, with respect to access to compute capacity across COLOSSUS and COLOSSUS II. Compute capacity provided includes approximately 325,000 NVIDIA GPUs, backed by hyperscale-class CPUs, exabyte-scale storage and high-speed networking and interconnects purpose-built for AI workloads. Pursuant to these agreements, the customer has agreed to pay us $1.25 billion per month through May 2029, with capacity ramping in May and June 2026 at a reduced fee.” ↩︎
  6. “Under the SpaceXAI Arrangements, we agreed to spend an aggregate of up to $120.5 billion over terms extending into 2029, consisting of approximately $3.1 billion in the aggregate per month once all capacity has been delivered, which we expect in December 2026, with different fees during capacity ramping periods.” ↩︎
  7. See our calculations and EpochAI’s calculations for more details. ↩︎

item.title: Toyota, Nissan, and Honda to Standardize Parts to Lower Costs (622 pts)
item.description:
URL: https://www.caranddriver.com/news/a74490092/toyota-nissan-honda-standardize-parts-lower-costs/, See on Hacker News

  • Toyota, Nissan, and Honda will begin standardizing some vehicle parts in an effort to lower production costs, according to a report by Automotive News.
  • The automakers will start with equalized quality criteria for steel, consistent protocols for plastics, and a universal color-coding scheme for wiring harnesses.
  • Discussions are starting with Japan’s domestic suppliers, though international suppliers will be looped in soon.

Japan’s three largest automakers have agreed to begin standardizing vehicle parts in an effort to reduce costs, according to Automotive News. The outlet reports that Japan Automobile Manufacturers Association chairman Koji Sato, who is also the vice chairman of Toyota, announced the decision at a news conference in Tokyo this week.

In the short term, the standardization efforts will begin with unified quality criteria for steel, consistent protocols for plastics and resins, and a universal color-coding scheme for wiring harnesses. In the long term, the Japan Automobile Manufacturers Association has plans to move to more components that cover the entire car. The three areas were chosen as the first to be standardized because they are parts that are generally not noticed by consumers, and they shouldn’t have an impact on any brand’s individual identity. All three are also areas that account for significant production costs for the automakers, meaning they can have an immediate impact.

The first discussions of standardization are set to include Japan’s domestic automotive parts suppliers, though international suppliers will be brought into the fold in time. The first standardization efforts are set to go into place next year, according to the AN report.

The push to simplify and lower costs comes as Japan’s seven automakers, including Toyota, Nissan, Honda, Mazda, Subaru, Mitsubishi, and Suzuki, work to fend off the increasingly competitive list of Chinese automakers. The automakers are said to hope that they can channel the money saved by homogenizing into new innovations.

“We all share this strong sense of crisis, creating a momentum for change,” Sato said. “Based upon our sense of a crisis, we decided to choose these three areas.”

➡️ Skip the lot. Let Car and Driver help you find your next car.

Jack Fitzgerald’s love for cars stems from his as yet unshakable addiction to Formula 1. After a brief stint as a detailer for a local dealership group in college, he knew he needed a more permanent way to drive all the new cars he couldn’t afford and decided to pursue a career in auto writing. By hounding his college professors at the University of Wisconsin-Milwaukee, he was able to travel Wisconsin seeking out stories in the auto world before landing his dream job at Car and Driver. His new goal is to delay the inevitable demise of his 2010 Volkswagen Golf.

item.title: Data Processing Incidents on Inference Providers (175 pts)
item.description:
URL: https://openrouter.ai/blog/announcements/data-processing-incidents-on-inference-providers/, See on Hacker News

Earlier this week, security researchers reported that certain inference providers had data compromised or otherwise shown evidence that their data policies were not being upheld. We have been collaborating closely with the researchers and with providers to understand the findings and encourage the providers to address them.

These findings did not show any breach or unauthorized access of OpenRouter. The results of this testing revealed new findings about specific inference providers. A live list of the security announcements we have received from providers is below.

As the operating layer between customers and a fast-moving ecosystem of models and providers, we take data policy enforcement very seriously. We have taken the following actions:

  • Off-boarded three providers from OpenRouter, based on the results of our investigations.
  • Removed 125 endpoints from Zero Data Retention (ZDR) eligibility. The removals included providers flagged by researchers, plus additional endpoints that we removed as a precautionary measure.
  • Notified all potentially affected customers.

The following work is underway:

  • We are adapting the researchers’ testing approach so we can run these checks on an ongoing basis.
  • We are conducting technical verification of network paths to identify instances where requests and responses may be being forwarded to third parties.
  • We are requiring appropriate assurances and validation before restoring ZDR eligibility to any endpoint removed in this review.

We are grateful for the Dragos report. As we integrate similar testing techniques into OpenRouter, we will keep raising the bar, and providers that want to be on OpenRouter will need to meet it.

Provider security announcements

  • Novita: Privacy notice regarding MiniMax requests on Novita
  • Phala: November preliminary incident report
  • Together: Security event: prompt leakage for requests in June and July of 2026

Not all affected providers have posted publicly. We have notified affected users regardless of whether there is a public post. We are encouraging all providers to create incident write-ups and will keep this list updated.

item.title: Leonida – PC Recompilation of the Xbox Version of GTA 6 (171 pts)
item.description:
URL: https://github.com/ItsNotRexed/Leonida, See on Hacker News

Grand Theft Auto VI (Xbox Series) running natively on Windows, built on your PC from your own copy.

Status | How to build | How it works | Want to help? | Credits | License | Discord

Leonida is a static recompilation project. The Xbox Series CPU is x86-64 like a PC, so the game's code is loaded and run natively, and the console's system software is reimplemented. The console's precompiled RDNA2 GPU programs are translated to SPIR-V for Vulkan. The game's models, textures and audio are read from your package. All of this happens on your PC, from your own copy of the game.

Important

This repository does not contain the game, keys or an executable, and it does not explain how to get them. You need your own copy, with its files already readable on disk. Nothing here decrypts or works around any protection. Everything the build creates (the generated shaders, extracted assets, the runtime folder and your saves) comes from your game and stays on your PC. Never share those files.

Discord: https://discord.gg/rexed

Project status

Early. The game does not boot yet. Everything that can be done without the game's executable is in place, so work on booting can start as soon as one is available to a developer.

What Status
Finding and checking your copy (Xbox Series 1.0.2.1) ✅ Works
Shaders: carve, unpack native RDNA2 code, disassemble ✅ All 26,503
Shaders: RDNA2 → SPIR-V translation ✅ All 26,503 (disassembled with LLVM 21; LLVM 23 leaves 1,471 rejected for now, #644): 2,236 VS, 12,101 PS, 2,689 CS, 9,282 mesh, 195 geometry. All pass spirv-val, with a per-shader metadata index for pipeline creation. ⚠️ 21,545 are wave64: exact on 64-wide subgroups (AMD). On 32-wide subgroups (NVIDIA, Intel), compute and mesh shaders are exact with wave64 emulation (--wave64-emulate, on by default there); cross-half wave ops in vertex, pixel and geometry shaders are still approximate
Shader translator checked on a real GPU ⚠️ The hand-written GPU tests (vertex fetch, texture sampling, exports, ALU ops, partial-register ops, barycentrics, wave-uniform branches, compute LDS/barriers/buffer stores, wave64 masks) have been run on more than 30 GPU and driver combinations, with results in #166: NVIDIA Turing, Ampere, Ada and Blackwell (Windows and Linux); AMD GCN3, RDNA1, RDNA2, RDNA3 and RDNA4 (Windows driver and RADV); Intel Gen9 (ANV); Apple M1 (MoltenVK, no geometry or mesh stages); and Mesa llvmpipe. Wave64 tests need 64-wide subgroups (AMD) or LEONIDA_W64_EMULATE=1. These are small test shaders: the game's own shaders are checked by spirv-val and by driver pipeline creation (vk_pipeline_check), not by their output
Models (OBJ with real names, UVs, material references) ✅ Exported. Not all layouts are decoded yet
Texture dictionaries and world texture pools (DDS) ✅ Exported. Pool entries stored as BCPack are still skipped by the export; a clean-room decoder (tools/bcpack.py) rebuilds BC1, BC3, BC4 and BC5, and is not wired into rpf9dump yet (notes)
Audio banks (AWC: Opus, XMA2) ✅ Exported whole. Opus repackaged losslessly as Ogg Opus; PCM (codec 0/2) as WAV; XMA2 decoded with ffmpeg. --wav adds 16-bit PCM WAV (notes)
Music/radio config ? Measured. 1,589 audio-config records with exact durations and AWC stream ids; station grouping and content-id lists; no per-track start offsets (notes)
PE loader and import shims ⚠️ Runs a stand-in executable end to end (gta6rt --run: CRT startup, statics, heap, files, threads, GDK imports through the shims, exit code back). Untested against the real executable
Xbox D3D12 → Vulkan ⚠️ In progress. A Vulkan-backed device behind the Xbox-ABI proxy creates queues, command lists, fences, descriptor heaps, committed and reserved resources, render-target and depth views, texture views and samplers (which go into the bindless set), and query heaps. Barriers, clears, uploads, copies (BC included), colour resolves and occlusion, timestamp and pipeline-statistics queries run on Vulkan, checked on one GPU. No buffer views, root signatures, pipelines, draws or swapchain yet (plan)
Booting, story mode, anything playable ❌ No

How to build

The port isn't downloaded ready-made. It's built on your PC from your own copy.

The easy way:

  1. Install the prerequisites below.
  2. Download this project with its submodule: git clone --recursive https://github.com/ItsNotRexed/Leonida. A "Download ZIP" from GitHub leaves out third_party/rpf9-explorer. The build fetches it if git is installed, and otherwise tells you what to do.
  3. Double-click Build.bat.

It finds your copy of the game by itself: it looks in Downloads, Desktop, Documents, Games, your home folder and the top of every drive, two folders deep. It recognises the version from a few file sizes, without reading anything large. If you have more than one copy it asks which one, and if it finds none it asks you to paste the folder. Before starting it checks that everything below is installed and that there is enough free space, and it lists anything missing in one go. The result goes to Documents\Leonida. A stopped build continues where it left off.

Your game folder is the one that holds MicrosoftGame.Config and the .rpf archives, as plain files.

Prerequisites:

  • Your own copy of the Xbox Series package, version 1.0.2.1.
  • Windows 10/11 x64, with about 350 GB free for work files. They can go on another drive with --work.
  • Python 3.12+ (tick "Add python.exe to PATH").
  • .NET 8 SDK.
  • Vulkan SDK, for spirv-as / spirv-val.
  • LLVM 21+ with the AMDGPU target for llvm-mc. The official Windows build has no AMDGPU target. On Windows, scripts\build_llvm_mc.ps1 builds a native llvm-mc.exe with it (no WSL; needs git and the Visual Studio C++ tools below) and sets LLVM_MC. Or install llvm-21 in WSL and set LLVM_MC to the whole command, LLVM_MC="wsl -d Ubuntu -e /usr/lib/llvm-21/bin/llvm-mc" (see docs/design.md). On Linux, llvm-mc on PATH is enough.
  • Visual Studio 2022 with Desktop development with C++ and the Windows SDK 10.0.26100 or newer, for the runtime stage (the runtime uses version 1.2 root signatures, which older SDKs don't declare).
  • ffmpeg on PATH (optional: decodes the XMA2 streams, and required for --wav).

From a terminal, with the same behaviour and more control:

python -I make_game.py --find                          # list the copies found on this PC
python -I make_game.py --check                         # check your copy, build nothing
python -I make_game.py --game "D:\path\to\your\package" --out "D:\Games\Leonida" --work "E:\leonida-work"
python -I make_game.py --stages shaders,assets         # only some stages
python -I make_game.py --game "D:\path\to\your\package" --wav   # also decode Opus to PCM WAV (large)
python -I make_game.py --wave64-emulate off            # auto (default), on or off; see below

--wave64-emulate decides whether wave64 compute and mesh shaders are translated to be exact on any subgroup size (see "Wave64 emulation" in docs/design.md). NVIDIA and Intel GPUs have 32-wide subgroups and need it. The default, auto, asks vulkaninfo (part of the Vulkan SDK) and turns it on unless every GPU reports 64-wide subgroups, or when it can't tell; it also turns it on when the GPU the runtime would use can't be made to run compute and mesh shaders 64-wide. The mode is saved next to the translated shaders, and changing it translates them again. With auto, a work folder that previously used emulation keeps it for later translations and retries, even if the current GPU supports native wave64. Use --wave64-emulate off to translate it natively.

The build records which translator sources produced the shaders. A change to those files reruns translation using the saved disassembly. Older work folders need one translation after upgrading to record this information.

Stages run in order: check, shaders, assets, runtime, pipelines (creates every translated shader on your GPU driver and saves a pipeline cache, so the first boot doesn't compile them). The shader translation is the longest step: it runs on --jobs processes (half the CPU threads by default).

--wav is off by default because 16-bit PCM WAV is several times larger than Ogg Opus. It decodes the repackaged Ogg Opus streams to work\assets\audio\wav after the audio bank step; existing WAV files are skipped when a build resumes.

Vulkan diagnostics on Linux

With CMake 3.24+, a C++20 compiler, and Vulkan development headers and loader installed:

cmake -S runtime -B runtime/build/linux
cmake --build runtime/build/linux --parallel
./runtime/build/linux/vk_pipeline_check /path/to/spirv

Pass the directory containing index.json and the translated SPIR-V files to vk_pipeline_check.

make_game.py runs on Linux too. The pipelines stage uses the vk_pipeline_check built above (runtime/build/linux, or runtime/build). The runtime stage builds on Windows only, so on Linux it needs a Windows build of runtime/; without one it is left out of the default stages, and asking for it fails before any work starts.

Running the loader on Linux

The loader is a Windows program and runs under Wine or Proton; CI runs its tests under Wine on every change to runtime/ (the wine job of the Runtime workflow). Give the runtime stage a folder with gta6rt.exe and gta6rt_tls_host.dll, such as the runtime-windows artifact of that workflow's windows job, unzipped:

python3 -I make_game.py --runtime-build ~/Downloads/runtime-windows

It copies both files into --out and writes gta6rt.sh next to them, which starts gta6rt.exe with wine, or with the Wine named by WINE (for Proton, its files/bin/wine). The same option skips the build on Windows.

How it works

Piece What it does Where
Version check Every package file's name, size and SHA-256 for each supported version game/, make_game.py
Shader pipeline Carves DXBC containers from shaders.rpf without its encrypted table of contents. Unpacks the XBCH → FSSM native RDNA2 program, disassembles it with LLVM (gfx1013) and translates it to SPIR-V tools/shader_carve.py, fssm_unpack.py, shader_disasm.py, rdna2spirv.py
Asset export Finds validated resources inside RPF9 archives and the loose .ttpf texture pools tools/rpf9dump (on rpf9-explorer's Core)
Runtime Maps the PE image, resolves imports to shims (GDK, XMem, d3d12_xs) runtime/
Research tools PE/RTTI inspection, raw carving, texture tiling probes, GPU test harnesses tools/, runtime/test/

The translator's runtime contract (user SGPRs, push constants, memory model, bindless images, vertex fetch, system values) and all the format notes are in docs/design.md; the format, asset, runtime and validation notes are indexed in docs/README.md. The Xbox D3D12 plan is in docs/d3d12_vulkan.md. Audio bank formats and the export tools are in docs/audio.md; docs/related_projects.md records the prior art we may read and the licence limits on it.

Want to help?

The biggest open pieces:

  • Shader translator on hardware: compute, mesh and geometry now translate (see the translator contract in docs/design.md); still open are the vertex-shader input layout (v0 = VertexIndex is unverified if the console runs VS as NGG) and wave64 cross-half code in VS/PS/GS on 32-wide subgroups.
  • Xbox D3D12 → Vulkan: the d3d12_xs command list and descriptor heap model.
  • Model layouts the decoder rejects today.

See CONTRIBUTING.md. Never attach game files, extracted assets or generated shaders to issues or pull requests.

Credits

  • rpf9-explorer by breadbbbb: the RPF9 model, texture-pool and AWC decoders used by tools/rpf9dump (git submodule).
  • Mesa (MIT): GFX10 resource-descriptor layout (tools/gfx10_formats.json), and the ACO/RADV rules used as reference for 16-bit results and shader system registers.
  • libHttpClient (MIT) by Microsoft: the XTaskQueue/XAsync implementation in third_party/xtaskqueue, used by the offline xgameruntime shim.
  • LLVM: AMDGPU disassembler.
  • Logo: "Grand Theft Auto VI" icon by SlyDevil on SteamGridDB.
  • SPIRV-Tools: assembly and validation.

item.title: PcapAnalyzer – self-hosted pcap analyzer with 27 problem detectors (127 pts)
item.description:
URL: https://github.com/sebaandrada-cell/PcapAnalyzer, See on Hacker News

Versión en español: README.es.md.

Find the network fault in seconds, not hours. Upload a .pcap / .pcapng capture (gzip too) and PcapAnalyzer tells you what is failing, why, and what to check next. It runs on your own machine, so captures never leave your network.

Free and open source (Apache 2.0). Status: beta.

  • Try it without installing anything: https://pcap-analyzer-seven.vercel.app/#demo
  • Download: https://sebaandrada6.gumroad.com/l/hspgx (free) or clone this repository.

What it does

  • 27 detectors that run on every capture, each with a severity and a next step:
    • TCP: firewall blocks (SYN→RST), retransmissions, duplicate ACKs, loss and reordering, zero and full windows, resets after the handshake, slow handshakes.
    • Path: PMTUD black holes, low MSS, IP fragmentation, ICMP errors, routing loops.
    • Name and address services: unanswered or slow DNS, SERVFAIL, NXDOMAIN bursts, DHCP NAK / DECLINE / no answer, duplicate IPs, ARP storms.
    • Applications: HTTP 4xx / 5xx and slow responses, TLS alerts, SSL 3.0 / TLS 1.0 / 1.1.
    • Tunnels: IPsec (IKE and ESP), WireGuard, OpenVPN, GRE, L2TP and Teredo that are one-way, never answer a handshake or keep renegotiating.
    • Security: port scans and sweeps, cleartext logins (FTP, POP3, IMAP, SMTP AUTH, HTTP Basic; credentials are never stored or shown), Telnet / SMBv1 / SNMP v1-v2c, ARP spoofing, overlapping IP fragments.
  • Capture quality first. It warns when the capture itself limits the result: frames duplicated by a mirror port, traffic seen in one direction only, truncated packets, connections already open when the capture started.
  • Wireshark-style views: packet list with real Wireshark display filters over the whole capture, colouring, CSV export, expert info, HTTP / DNS / DHCP / TLS tables, response times and a flow diagram per conversation.
  • AI investigation (optional): an AI investigates the capture with tools (real filters, stream detail, statistics) and cites the packets behind every claim. You can then ask follow-up questions. It uses your own Anthropic API key; without one, a demo mode runs the full flow with text generated from the analysis, at no cost.
  • PDF report, Spanish and English interface, light and dark theme.

Quick start

You need Docker with Docker Compose. On Windows, run the script from Git Bash or WSL.

git clone https://github.com/sebaandrada-cell/PcapAnalyzer.git
cd PcapAnalyzer
./start.sh

The script creates a random access token (shown once, stored in .env) and starts the app. When the build finishes, open http://localhost:8080, paste the token into the "API token" field (top right) and upload a capture, or click "Try the sample capture".

The app listens on 127.0.0.1 only. Do not expose it on a network without an authenticated reverse proxy: the API can use your AI account. QUICKSTART.md has the details, the AI setup and troubleshooting.

Without Docker

You need Python 3.9+, Node 20+ and tshark (installed with Wireshark).

cd backend
python3 -m venv .venv
.venv/bin/pip install -r requirements-dev.txt
export API_TOKENS="$(openssl rand -hex 32)"
.venv/bin/uvicorn app.main:app --reload
cd frontend
npm install
npm run dev

Open http://localhost:5173 and paste the same token. If tshark is not on your PATH, set TSHARK_PATH to the binary.

Privacy

  • The capture is analysed on your machine. While an AI investigation lasts it is kept encrypted (60 minutes of inactivity, or until you press "Delete capture now") and is then deleted.
  • The AI is optional. It only sees what its tools return (packet metadata; packet content only if you switch it on for that session), never the pcap file.
  • No telemetry and no accounts for the self-hosted version.

Tests

cd backend && .venv/bin/python -m pytest -q    # needs tshark
cd frontend && npm test

Feedback

PcapAnalyzer is a beta. It has been tested with synthetic fixtures and public sample captures, and the most useful feedback is a capture where it misses a problem or reports one that is not real. Please open an issue at https://github.com/sebaandrada-cell/PcapAnalyzer/issues and describe the case. Do not attach captures that contain real credentials or customer data; anonymise them first or describe the pattern.

The technical reference (JSON schema, detector thresholds, limits, API errors) is in README.es.md, in Spanish.

item.title: Advice for the next 100 Rust GUIs (188 pts)
item.description:
URL: https://linebender.org/blog/next-100-guis/, See on Hacker News

Raph Levien, November 21, 2026

This is a followup to Advice for the next dozen Rust GUIs, published 4.5 years ago. The world is different in many ways, but some of the advice there is still valid. There have been roughly 20 Rust GUI toolkits announced since that blog post (see 2026 survey), but also a recent rapid acceleration of interest in Rust GUI, fueled by AI.

Rust GUI is still compelling

The motivation to build GUI apps in Rust remains strong. Many shipping GUI apps suffer from poor performance, especially when built with cross-platform technology. GUI toolkits shipped by platforms have largely stagnated, and system vendors remain uninterested in solving the cross-platform problem, so Electron has grown in popularity. RAM remains expensive and the focus is shifting to mobile, so bloat has real consequences. Building high-performance UI in Rust is a practical alternative.

Adoption of Rust UI in the past few years has been slow. Few flagship apps use Rust for their UI. One of the most notable is the Zed editor, built on their own GPUI framework. It proves that shipping Rust UI is practical, and indeed, GPUI is emerging as a major choice for AI-driven rewrites, most notably Discord. My personal sense is that GPUI is well suited to the Zed use case, and shipping in a real project boosts its visibility and credibility quite a bit, but it’s not necessarily the ideal choice for more general purpose applications. Among other things, its 2D rendering engine is well suited to a text editor, but lacks full gradient support, blending, filters, and other features expected of a renderer in the same class as Vello or Skia.

The reasons for slow adoption may be melting away. Writing Rust code is harder than languages more traditionally used for UI (TypeScript, Kotlin, Swift), and finding engineers skilled in both Rust and UI is challenging. But AI is changing the game. There’s evidence that the LLM cost of writing Rust code is not significantly higher than other languages, and there is reason to believe that in large codebases, Rust will be more maintainable because its type system helps enforce invariants. So if all languages have roughly the same cost, then why not go with one that has a dramatically better combination of safety and performance?

For these reasons, Rust is rapidly becoming the language for AI rewrites of existing codebases. But there is still no consensus on the strategy for the UI layer. I predict there will be a small explosion of trying lots of different things.

Native is complicated

My 2022 blog post had a large section on “native,” first pointing out that the term has no clear meaning, and more broadly pointing out that “native” UI toolkits are simply choices among many, and should be evaluated on the important quality criteria.

I think this is largely still true, but it depends greatly on which platform is being targeted. Windows still has no clear native choice (see Microsoft Hasn’t Had a Coherent GUI Strategy Since Petzold) and on Mac there is a bit of fragmentation between AppKit and SwiftUI. However, SwiftUI has performance issues (see Michael Tsai blog from 2025) and so it is clearly possible to do better on the performance front.

While desktop UI has remained stagnant, the situation on mobile is a bit different. Platforms continue to invest, and there are many fine details that are important for an app to look and feel native. One very notable example is Liquid Glass on iOS – if you use UIKit or SwiftUI, you can get that with little effort, but apps built with cross-platform toolkits won’t quite seem right. In addition, making gesture recognition, scroll dynamics, and IME 100% match the platform are not yet fully solved problems.

Thus, for mobile, an extremely viable path is to use the native toolkit for UI but do the common “business logic” in Rust. I’m not sure about the business logic, but for the UI, this is the decision that Shopify has made recently, abandoning React Native. I believe 1Password has this architecture. This is also the "Phoenix" plan for Discord on mobile, while using GPUI on desktop.

That said, there's been considerable progress in trying to build mobile UI entirely in Rust. Below is a short screencast of the editor demo in android-view. You can see that a lot of IME functionality works, including swiping, moving the cursor by rolling the space bar, and deleting in semantic chunks. Not shown in the video below, but composition regions (needed for CJK) also work, and there's basic accessibility through AccessKit.

Text layout and accessibility infrastructure is basically solved

One of the big unsolved problems as of the 2022 blog post was text layout. It is of course a hard problem to get right. I’m pleased to say that the ecosystem now has a good solution, in the form of Parley. It’s gotten there as a result of sustained investment from Google, Canva, and Dioxus (now Cognition), as well as contributions from the community. It seems to be used in the majority of new Rust UI toolkits. In addition, to help mitigate the risk of monoculture, Cosmic Text is a viable alternative.

AccessKit was just getting started in 2022, but is now solid infrastructure as well, and used by most UI toolkits. I should note, though, there is a difference between a good integration and a box ticking exercise. And there is more work to be done, for example to make rich text editing fully accessible. One other problem I'd like to see addressed is performance degradation when accessibility is enabled. This is a problem for egui in particular, as it has to build and diff a tree each animation frame, undercutting the benefits of its underlying immediate mode design.

System compositor is still unsolved

One topic I talked about extensively in the 2022 blog post is leveraging the system compositor. This issue is even more pressing today, especially with the increased importance of video. You really want a video playing in a hardware accelerated layer when possible, and on low end devices it’s the only hope for getting smooth frame rates.

There has been some progress, notably the subduction library, but it certainly isn’t commonly integrated into UI toolkits yet. To do it well is a challenging problem, as the capabilities provided by the platform vary widely. Ideally there’s a rich and high level interface, something like CALayer on Apple platforms, and polyfills to implement that interface as well as possible on other platforms. On Android, when the task is something simple, like overlaying some GUI controls on a video, it would use SurfaceFlinger layers, but when it involves more sophisticated compositing, it would run shaders on the GPU.

This is absolutely something we should build, ideally as a high quality community project rather than something with dozens of vibe-coded forks. But even in the latter case it’s better for it to exist than not.

One of the challenges of the Rust UI ecosystem is that different applications have different needs. The idea of a single, unified UI for completely general purpose use may be behind us, especially now that LLMs can optimize and fine tune for specific use cases.

That’s been playing out architecturally in the choice between immediate mode and retained mode. Immediate mode is very appealing because it’s less total code and seems quite a bit simpler. And for some applications (most especially development support for games) it works well. However, I am concerned it won’t scale especially well. In short, it’s good at the first 90%, but it makes the second 90% harder. To be considered really production-ready, it has to establish stable widget identities to build and update the accessibility tree, and it has to reliably cache expensive intermediate artifacts such as text layouts (simple immediate mode often gets around this by cutting corners in text layout, which may be fine for gamedev). And of course, it pulls strongly towards a model of re-rendering everything every frame rather than exploiting layers in the compositor.

For this reason among others, I am not impressed by the choice of the ArtCraft projects to use egui. I do think egui is a really good implementation of the immediate mode paradigm in Rust, and it does solve a number of problems (including accessibility, something mainline Iced does not yet support), but it wouldn’t be my first choice for productivity and design applications. The egui README is quite honest on the advantages and disadvantages, and is worth consulting.

Clearly defined modules

One theme that’s emerging from trying to do LLM-assisted software engineering well is having clearly scoped modules, ideally with solid specifications of what the module does. Within a module, given clear objectives such as performance and robustness against adverse inputs, an LLM can do very well.

This philosophy is in tension with what has historically worked well. People reasonably choose a UI toolkit based on how good it looks. In particular, Apple UI frameworks have an immense amount of design knowledge baked in, especially in the defaults. With very little effort, it’s possible for a developer to make an app that looks and feels like a Mac app, even if not very polished.

I think in the future we should be moving toward a separation of design and execution. Both are hard problems, but very different. I’m especially excited about how much room there is to improve the execution side when really optimizing. As discussed in the 2022 blog post, the computer science core of a UI toolkit is an incremental computation engine.

Having a good spec at the interface between design and execution is critically important. As a general strategy, I suggest adapting web standards, but not following them slavishly. Web standards are an impressive and important artifact. A huge amount of time and energy has gone into producing them, and there’s also a lot of care to making things work cross-platform. The extensive WPT tests are the true magic of the spec, aiding correctness in the multiple high quality open source implementations. All this goes a long way to explaining why Electron is popular.

That said, strictly adhering to web standards has serious downsides. DOM is slow and memory-intensive; a lighter weight tree representation with a bulk mutation interface might serve the need of GUI apps better. Full CSS style resolution and layout is also expensive, though CSS is a rich and powerful way to describe styling. A subset of CSS carefully curated for efficiency might be useful. I’ve done experiments in implementing selectors as an efficient state machine that supports incremental evaluation, at the expense of fancier CSS features such as sibling selectors.

The Web is also lacking a solid way to represent virtualized lists, a core feature of every efficient UI toolkit. A spec here requires nailing down the interface with the data model, preserving incrementality.

Blitz, as a modular browser engine, is well placed to serve as the cornerstone of hybrid approaches borrowing heavily from Web specs, but also adapting them to be higher performance and more tightly integrated with platform capabilities. As just one example, it’s possible to start with Stylo as the CSS selector engine, and then replace it with a leaner, more efficient CSS engine if that proves to be practical.

One good example of separation of concerns into smaller modules is the Xilem/Masonry split. The Xilem reactive layer was designed to be independent of the actual elements it controls, and indeed it has instantiations both for DOM (which, among other things, is the infrastructure for the squircle interactive demo) and Masonry widgets. Masonry, on the other hand, was designed to be independent of the reactive layer and indeed the language for the layer above it.

By contrast, SwiftUI mashes together the low level widget implementation, the reactivity framework, and the language as well; Swift runtime reflection is part of the execution engine. Obviously SwiftUI has had a lot farther reach than Xilem, but my argument today is that we should reconsider assumptions as things are rapidly changing.

Optimization opportunities

Given a UI design encoded in a certain way – which can be code, data, or a combination of the two in a DSL – an engine has a number of opportunities to optimize the execution of that design. Perhaps a lot of this section is gilding the lily, as a straightforward evaluation of the design in optimized Rust code will outperform almost any shipping GUI. But I’m interested in the limits of what performance is possible. Can we get silky smooth UI even on low end Android phones? I think the answer is yes, and the question worth exploring.

One useful tactic may be separating out the static from the dynamic parts of the design, and precomputing the static parts. That in no way precludes the design having dynamic parts; it's just that it may be possible to avoid the cost of a fully dynamic implementation.

Another fruitful avenue for optimization is optimizing the use of layers, to be composited either using the system compositor or a lightweight GPU-accelerated polyfill. Using layers effectively can dramatically improve performance, mostly by avoiding re-rendering of parts of the interface that haven't changed. However, layers have a RAM cost, and using too many layers can actually slow things down, as allocating new layers has to go through calls to the underlying system. Getting this right is a tricky optimization problem, and a good use of either measurement or analysis. UI toolkits generally either use heuristics, which are not always perfect, or explicit hints (like .drawingGroup() in SwiftUI or RepaintBoundary in Flutter).

For a deeper dive into performance questions, see A Critique of GPUI. Ideally, there aren't huge performance differences between UI toolkits, as all low hanging fruit should be picked. We expect implementations of system languages to be quite comparable in performance, but still tolerate wide discrepancies in GUI performance.

Advice

  • Be bold. Now is the time. Rust UI has the potential to deliver vastly higher performance than the status quo.
  • Build on solid foundations.
  • Use well-defined specs when available.
  • Find ways to work well with open source. Work with upstream but don’t spam them with slop PRs.

Acknowledgements

Thanks to Nico Burns for reviewing an earlier draft of this post.

A use-after-free in Ghostscript’s Type 1 font loader lets a crafted document cross Ghostscript’s -dSAFER sandbox, alter native path controls, and execute attacker-chosen commands as the rendering process.

Ghostscript sits beneath print, email, upload, and preview workflows. Our ImageMagick research showed how files named .png or .jpg can still reach Ghostscript through image conversion. The index below records confirmed affected paths alongside additional applications whose renderer routes we traced.

Upload2Shell / public record

Disclosure sequence

From the first escape to the downstream reports, fixes, and publication.

  1. 27 JUL 2026DISCOVERY

    Upload2Shell

    We found a Type 1 font-loader path out of Ghostscript's -dSAFER boundary. A crafted document gained native access inside the rendering process.

  2. BY 30 JULGOOGLE PROOF

    Google's image and document pipeline

    A signed-out request for an attacker-hosted file reached Ghostscript in Google's document renderer. We sent the production proof to Google.

  3. 12 AUG 2026WORDPRESS FIX

    WordPress Core

    Core's upload path exposed the renderer to Author+ users and any Contributor granted upload_files. Public upload fields in multiple plugins required no WordPress login. WordPress shipped its separate CVE-2026-65640 fix.

item.title: Inkling-2-Mini in 5.4 GB Memory (482 pts)
item.description:
URL: https://github.com/ShinMegamiBoson/lookatmyquant, See on Hacker News

LookAtMyQuant is a quantization compiler. It measures how much each stored piece of a model hurts the output when compressed. It then picks a code for each piece so the whole model fits a size budget with the least damage.

On Gemma 4 E2B, its GGUF has 12× lower KL than Q4_K_M at the same file size. The method and every result are on the site.

The code is under the MIT license.

LookAtMyQuant 2: Qwen3.5-4B in 1.2 GB

LookAtMyQuant 2 takes Qwen3.5-4B to 1.23 GB, 2.3 bits per weight. The file solves 330 of 540 exact-answer math problems. Prism ML's Bonsai 2 Ternary 4B solves 328 at 1.20 GB, and the original solves 359. Its KL from the original on held-out text is 0.45 nats, against 0.59 for Bonsai.

The recipe is post-training quantization with trellis codes, calibrated on the model's own worked math solutions with digit tokens weighted 10×, and with bits allocated per row by Fisher information. 4,000 steps of distillation follow, in which every layer is re-quantized once from the original weights. The page has the findings, the full recipe and its cost, about $34 of GPU time.

The recipe's code is here, and the next section runs it. The 1.23 GB file itself is the lm2-qwen35-4b-1.2gb release, packed for the Apple Silicon runtime.

Qwen3.8-27B in 7.2 GB

The same recipe takes Qwen3.8-27B from 53.7 GB to 7.2 GB, 2.1 bits per weight, calibrated and distilled on English prose and chat, code and math. The file solves 401 of the 540 math problems, as many as the original, and Unsloth's UD-IQ2_XXS GGUF of the same size solves 348. It also scores above that GGUF on HumanEval (73.8% against 67.1%), MMLU (78.8% against 75.0%) and GSM8K (94.5% against 92.7%).

Beside it sits a 4-bit DSpine drafter (1.02 GB, converted from tencent/Qwen3.8-27B-DSpine-b16 with runtime_mlx/convert_dspine.py and packed with pack_drafter.py), which roughly doubles decode speed on math and code on Apple silicon.

Inkling-2-Mini in 5.4 GB and 8.9 GB

The same compiler and proximal fine-tuning (SQYFR), extended to a 26.4B physical / 5.4B active 3×-looped MoE (L6–17 looped 3× = 48 logical visits, 128 experts top-8), compresses thinkingmachines/Inkling-2-Mini from 18.89 GB of text weights to 5.38 GB (1.63 bits/weight) and 8.87 GB (2.69 bits/weight) using 4 KB SRAM hashed block-vector trellis codes (ht2/ht3), row trellis codes (rtr1/rtr4), and a tr2 floor on the tail lm_head bucket (head.7).

Evaluated on the same BF16 teacher, openai/gsm8k (test[:200], greedy, reasoning_effort="none"), all 164 executable openai/openai_humaneval problems, 4 Vision VQA tests (with the untouched 637 MB BF16 vision tower), and 16+13-language TextMix windows:

Model Text GB free_KL (en/chat/code) all13_KL GSM8K (200) HumanEval (164) Pooled vs Teacher
Original BF16 Teacher 18.89 0.0000 0.0000 147 / 200 (73.5%) 66 / 164 (40.2%) 100.0%
LookAtMyQuant 5.4 GB (SQYFR) 5.38 0.0895 0.2871 134 / 200 (67.0%) 60 / 164 (36.6%) 91.2%
Unsloth UD-IQ1_S 7.76 0.0808 0.1236 127 / 200 (63.5%) 46 / 164 (28.0%) 81.6%
LookAtMyQuant 8.9 GB (SQYFR) 8.87 0.0208 0.0571 148 / 200 (74.0%) 58 / 164 (35.4%) 96.8%
Unsloth UD-Q2_K_XL 9.14 0.0486 0.0811 132 / 200 (66.0%) 49 / 164 (29.9%) 85.3%
Unsloth UD-IQ3_XXS 11.66 0.0189 0.0278 148 / 200 (74.0%) 68 / 164 (41.5%) 101.4%

At 5.38 GB, Inkling-2-Mini-LookAtMyQuant-5.4GB outscores Unsloth's 9.14 GB UD-Q2_K_XL on both GSM8K and HumanEval at 41% smaller size (up from 76/200 and 24/164 untuned). At 8.87 GB, Inkling-2-Mini-LookAtMyQuant-8.9GB matches the BF16 original on GSM8K and cuts KL 2.34× on English/chat/code and 29.6% across all 13 languages below UD-Q2_K_XL. Both run directly through lamq and runtime_mlx with custom Apple Silicon Metal kernels (including M5 MetalPerformancePrimitives MoE prefill + FlashAttention-2 SDPA + exact unbiased temp > 0 speculative sampling, plus opt-in dynamic sigmoid Top-K routing, tight-margin verify, and N-gram prompt lookup), optionally paired with the 178.9 MB 4-bit DSpark drafters: on M5 Max, 5.4 GB reaches 1,807 tok/s T=512 prefill (1,047 tok/s at T=128), 75.3 tok/s serial decode, and 124.4 tok/s median lossless drafted decode (142.9 tok/s math, 126.5 tok/s reasoning, 122.2 tok/s code, 104.0 tok/s prose; up to ~150–160 tok/s with opt-in top6 / max_logit_gap=0.30; 5.98 GB active RAM), and 8.9 GB decodes at 63.5 tok/s serial and 106.0 tok/s median (125.8 tok/s reasoning, 123.8 tok/s math; 9.41 GB active RAM).

Install and use the Apple Silicon runtime

On Apple silicon, install the runtime package directly (this installs mlx, mlx-lm, numpy, and huggingface-hub without the PyTorch compiler dependencies):

pip install git+https://github.com/ShinMegamiBoson/lookatmyquant.git

From a local clone, pip install -e . installs the lamq command, or run python -m runtime_mlx without installing.

Command line. Pass either a local model folder or a Hugging Face repo ID:

lamq generate shinmegamiboson/Qwen3.8-27B-LookAtMyQuant-7.2GB \
    -p "What is 17 times 23? Show the steps."

lamq generate shinmegamiboson/Qwen3.8-27B-LookAtMyQuant-7.2GB \
    --drafter shinmegamiboson/Qwen3.8-27B-LookAtMyQuant-7.2GB-drafter \
    -p "Write a Python function that merges overlapping intervals." --stats

lamq chat shinmegamiboson/Qwen3.8-27B-LookAtMyQuant-7.2GB \
    --drafter shinmegamiboson/Qwen3.8-27B-LookAtMyQuant-7.2GB-drafter

lamq generate shinmegamiboson/Inkling-2-Mini-LookAtMyQuant-5.4GB \
    --drafter shinmegamiboson/Inkling-2-Mini-LookAtMyQuant-drafter \
    -p "What is 17 times 23? Show the steps." --stats

lamq generate reads stdin when -p is omitted, supports --raw, --system, --thinking, --temp, --mode linear|chat-fork|copy-wide, --no-adaptive, and --json. lamq info <model> inspects a packed model's format and dimensions without loading weights.

Python integration. runtime_mlx.load returns an (model, tokenizer) pair compatible with mlx_lm.generate and mlx_lm.stream_generate (auto-detecting opgraph-packed-1 models such as Qwen3.5-4B / Qwen3.8-27B and lamq.json exports such as Gemma 4 E2B):

from mlx_lm import generate
from runtime_mlx import load

model, tok = load("shinmegamiboson/Qwen3.8-27B-LookAtMyQuant-7.2GB")
prompt = tok.apply_chat_template(
    [{"role": "user", "content": "What is 17 times 23? Show the steps."}],
    add_generation_prompt=True,
    enable_thinking=False,
)
print(generate(model, tok, prompt, max_tokens=200))

For streaming, multi-turn chat, or speculative decoding through one interface, use Runtime:

from runtime_mlx import Runtime

rt = Runtime.load(
    "shinmegamiboson/Qwen3.8-27B-LookAtMyQuant-7.2GB",
    drafter="shinmegamiboson/Qwen3.8-27B-LookAtMyQuant-7.2GB-drafter",
)
for chunk in rt.stream("Solve 3x + 4y = 31 and 5x - 2y = 17.", max_tokens=256):
    print(chunk.text, end="", flush=True)

Run the compiler on SmolLM2-360M in three commands

Install the dependencies and download the model and WikiText-2. The code reads SmolLM2-360M's config when it starts, so do this first.

pip install -r requirements.txt
python -c "from huggingface_hub import snapshot_download as d; d('HuggingFaceTB/SmolLM2-360M')"
python -c "from datasets import load_dataset as l; l('Salesforce/wikitext', 'wikitext-2-raw-v1')"

Measure. This compresses one piece at a time, leaves the rest exact, and records the KL to the original model. The full set for this model, 2,312 measurements, took about 50 minutes on an L40S.

python compiler.py measure --model HuggingFaceTB/SmolLM2-360M --part linear --layers 0-3 --out results/batch/my_measurements.json

Allocate. This picks one code per piece, with the least summed KL inside the budget. It needs no GPU. This command uses the SmolLM2-360M measurements in this repository, with a budget of 3.044 bits per weight.

python compiler.py allocate --sens 'results/batch/ccSens*.json' --target disk --items linear --bits 3.044 --out results/compiler/plans/my_plan.json

The plan it writes has the same widths as results/compiler/plans/sm_lin_3044.json.

Build and score. This quantizes the model to the plan, one matrix at a time. It then reports perplexity and KL to the original on WikiText-2 test.

python quantize.py --program plan --model HuggingFaceTB/SmolLM2-360M --plan results/compiler/plans/my_plan.json --out results/my_run.json

Our run of that plan is in results/batch/cc_sm_lin_3044.json. It reached perplexity 16.64 and KL 0.0926, against an original perplexity of 15.31. Add --layers 1 --calib 8 --eval 2 for a quick check that everything works.

Run the LookAtMyQuant 2 recipe on Qwen3.5-4B

Each step is a named job; python run_batch.py --list prints its command. The jobs need Qwen3.5-4B in models/Qwen3.5-4B on the volume and the text mix (modal run --detach modal_fetch.py --text). Every file they make goes to lm2/ on the volume.

modal run --detach modal_app.py --jobs lm2Text
modal run --detach modal_app.py --jobs lm2Calibration,lm2Solutions
modal run --detach modal_app.py --jobs lm2RowImportance
modal run --detach modal_app.py --jobs lm2Build
modal run --detach modal_app.py --jobs lm2Finetune
modal run --detach modal_app.py --jobs lm2Math,lm2Math216,lm2TextKL
Job Script What it does Our run
lm2Text other_text.py The original answers science, code, instruction and tool prompts, and MATH and GSM8K training problems. This also downloads MATH
lm2Calibration math_calibration.py The calibration set: the original's greedy solutions to 384 MATH training problems, in 2,048-token windows 15 minutes, H100
lm2Solutions checked_solutions.py The math text the fine-tuning distils on: solutions to MATH problems and to math_bench.py problems from another seed, with wrong calculations corrected and only right answers kept 33 minutes, H100
lm2RowImportance row_importance.py Each output row's Fisher information at digit-predicting positions 1 minute, H100
lm2Build quantize.py Post-training quantization: trellis codes along rows, digit tokens weighted 10× in the Hessians, QEP at α = 0.5, bits per row from the row plan, e-means codebooks 37 minutes, H100
lm2Finetune finetune.py 4,000 steps of distillation on latent weights pulled toward their codes, with every layer re-quantized once from the original weights 2.7 hours, B200
lm2Math, lm2Math216 math_eval.py The 540-problem benchmark and a second set of 216, for the original, Bonsai, the build and the fine-tuned build 20 minutes a model, H100
lm2TextKL text_kl.py KL from the original on WikiText-2 and on the text mix's 13 sources 1 minute a model, H100

lm2BuildSmoke, lm2FinetuneSmoke and lm2MathSmoke run the same code on two layers, 60 steps and 36 problems, in a few minutes each.

The row plan. lm2Build reads results/compiler/rows/q35_rowplan_1p2GB.json, which gives 1 to 4 bits to each of 1,520 row groups. row_allocation.py made it. Its build-control command builds and packs a control with a fixed split of rows, prepare-rows allocates rows inside the control's packed bytes with rowgroup_alloc.py, and build-rows builds under the plan and checks the packed size against it.

The codebooks. The four e-means codebooks the build decodes with are in cache/codes/. --trellis-fit lloyd gives the earlier ones, and a plan made before the change keeps them unless the flag says otherwise.

Recent equal-byte recipe improvements. Two zero-byte additions are available in the compiler and fine-tuning scripts:

  • Softmax-Fisher token table ranking (--embed-order sfisher-mix in compiler.py measure and quantize.py). Ranks tied embedding/output buckets by a 50/50 blend of output Softmax-Fisher E[p_v (1 - p_v)] and corpus frequency (and untied output heads by Softmax-Fisher alone).
  • Mid-training equal-byte row reallocation (--realloc-at 1000 in finetune.py). Paired with --rebuild-at 1000, measures each layer's continuous-vs-stored proximal KL gap KL(all P) - KL(layer = W) to shift bits toward deep unabsorbed layers while keeping exact file size (--realloc-max-delta 1). Combined with sfisher-mix on Qwen3.5-4B at identical 1.23 GB (2.297 bpp), WikiText-2 KL fell from 0.425 to 0.387 (−9.0%) and 13-source KL from 0.447 to 0.378 (−15.5%, improving all 13 sources).

Where these jobs differ from our run. Our GSM8K solutions were written earlier, with thinking always off. Our text KL on 13 sources used 52 windows picked from the text mix by a separate tool; --sources mix takes the mix's own evaluation windows, on which our file scores 0.44 where the page reports 0.45.

Large models run on Modal, one GPU per job

run_batch.py names every job, and modal_app.py runs them. modal_fetch.py downloads models and the text mix used for calibration and evaluation.

modal run modal_app.py::setup
modal run --detach modal_fetch.py --text
modal run --detach modal_fetch.py --models google/gemma-4-E2B-it
modal run --detach modal_app.py --jobs ccMG4E2Noise,ccMG4E2Spot,ccMG4E2EmbKv

The runs behind the site used these machines, each with 8 CPU cores:

Model GPU Time
SmolLM2-360M L40S About 50 minutes to measure, in 9 parallel jobs
Gemma 4 E2B, measuring H100 7–26 minutes per job, in 4 jobs
Gemma 4 E2B, building a plan H100 28–58 minutes per plan

gguf_compiler.py makes plans out of llama.cpp's own tensor types, so the result runs in llama.cpp as it is. public_eval.py scores public quantizations the same way as our plans. Both run inside the image in modal_gguf.py, which builds llama.cpp with CUDA.

The Apple Silicon runtime reads Lloyd–Max and trellis plans

quantize.py --export <folder> writes a plan in the format runtime_mlx/ reads. A plan with trellis codes also needs --trellis-rows 16,8, which runs each trellis path along a row of its matrix, so that decoding an entry reads only that row. On Apple silicon, pip install . installs mlx and mlx-lm; requirements.txt holds the PyTorch compiler dependencies.

On Gemma 4 E2B at 2.5 GB, the trellis plan has 26% lower KL than the Lloyd–Max plan and decodes about 22% slower. runtime_mlx/test_trellis_gen.py and runtime_mlx/test_trellis.py check the trellis kernels against the matrices the quantizer built.

python runtime_mlx/bench.py lamq path/to/export

A drafter makes the 1.2 GB file generate 1.5 to 2 times faster on Apple silicon

runtime_mlx/fast_q35.py decodes the packed 1.2 GB Qwen3.5-4B file one token at a time, straight from its trellis codes. runtime_mlx/drafter_q35.py adds speculative decoding. A small drafter proposes the seven tokens after the model's latest one in a single pass. The model then checks all eight positions in one pass over its coded weights (runtime_mlx/block_q35.py) and keeps the proposals that match its own choice, so the text is exactly its own greedy text.

On an M5 Max, over 30 held-out prompts of up to 256 tokens, generation with the drafter was 2.0 times as fast: 176 tokens a second against 88, timed in alternation in one process on 2026-11-11. A check kept 4.3 tokens on average. Over eight everyday prompts it was 1.5 times as fast. The gain follows how predictable the text is: 2.5 times on algebra, 2.0 on code, 1.2 on chat and 1.05 on a story, and one of the 30 held-out prompts ran slower with the drafter. The text matched plain greedy decoding on every prompt. These are speeds after the first token; reading the prompt takes about 0.1 s either way.

Two later changes are in this code. Each was measured against the version before it on 40 paired generations: proposing from the 96,033 most common tokens was 6.0% faster, and picking the winning token inside the packed product was 5.3% faster. Linear mode also enables self-calibrating adaptive fallback by default (adaptive=True; pass --no-adaptive to disable): when rolling acceptance drops below the measured break-even ratio of drafted-check latency to serial-step latency (accounting for cache flush and drafter context replay), it pauses drafting for short exact serial bursts and resumes once acceptance recovers, preserving bit-exact greedy parity while avoiding slowdowns on low-acceptance prose.

The drafter is a DSpine model, trained with SpecForge from the published DFlash drafter for Qwen3.5-4B on the 1.2 GB file's own greedy answers. modal_drafter.py runs the training as one Modal job, and it cost $42. On 300 held-out prompts the trained drafter gets 4.65 tokens per check, against 4.30 for the stock DFlash drafter.

pack_drafter.py stores the drafter at 4 bits a weight in the build's own code, with no calibration data: 464 MB against 1.83 GB at 16 bits. On 60 held-out prompts the 4-bit drafter kept 4.35 tokens per check against 4.38, and the text was the same. drafter_q35.py loads either form and writes the packed one out dense as it loads. The 4-bit drafter is the lm2-drafter-4bit release. It runs beside the packed 1.2 GB file, the lm2-qwen35-4b-1.2gb release.

gh release download lm2-qwen35-4b-1.2gb --repo ShinMegamiBoson/lookatmyquant -D q35-1.2gb
gh release download lm2-drafter-4bit --repo ShinMegamiBoson/lookatmyquant -D drafter-4bit
python runtime_mlx/bench_drafted.py q35-1.2gb drafter-4bit

The benchmark defaults to linear verification. Use --mode chat-fork to try a second candidate at an ambiguous early position, or --mode copy-wide for known contiguous copies. Copy mode uses the source cursor and tunes the gate/up and down projections for 16-slot checks. Both modes verify all emitted tokens with the packed target. To benchmark the chat fork, run:

python runtime_mlx/bench_drafted.py q35-1.2gb drafter-4bit --mode chat-fork --prompts chat

For a copy benchmark, pass --mode copy-wide --heldout path/to/copy-prompts.json. The JSON entries carry source, prompt_len, and input_ids from the packed model's tokenizer.

The checks, and the packer for a drafter of your own:

python runtime_mlx/test_fast_q35.py
LAMQ_Q35_PACKED=path/to/packed python runtime_mlx/test_block_q35.py
python runtime_mlx/check_drafter.py path/to/packed path/to/drafter
python runtime_mlx/bench_drafted.py path/to/packed path/to/drafter --heldout path/to/drafter/heldout/heldout.json --take 30
python pack_drafter.py path/to/drafter path/to/drafter-4bit

runtime_mlx/pack_dense.py writes the packed file from the fine-tuned build's dense weights, and runtime_mlx/modal_pack.py runs it on Modal. check_drafter.py compares the drafter in MLX with SpecForge's own model on reference blocks that drafter/reference.py writes.

The tests need SmolLM2-360M and WikiText-2

Each test file runs on its own from the repository root, and all seven finish in under a minute.

python tests/test_frame.py
python tests/test_grammar.py
python tests/test_codes.py
python tests/test_elements.py
python tests/test_nested.py
python tests/test_rowgroup_alloc.py
python tests/test_reallocation.py

runtime_mlx/test_core.py checks the runtime against the quantizer's math. Run python runtime_mlx/make_ref.py first, which writes 1.6 GB of reference files.

runtime_mlx/test_fast_q35.py and runtime_mlx/test_block_q35.py check the Qwen3.5 kernels against NumPy products of independently unpacked codes, with no model. When LAMQ_Q35_PACKED names a packed file, the second also checks a block of tokens against decoding them one at a time. When LAMQ_Q38_PACKED names the packed Qwen3.8-27B file, it runs the same checks on a model whose output head is stored apart from its embedding.

What this repository leaves out

item.title: PostgreSQL Extensions in Go (157 pts)
item.description:
URL: https://jespino.github.io/gopgext/, See on Hacker News

gopgext builds PostgreSQL extensions from plain Go code, using TinyGo. Mark a function with //gopgext:function and it becomes a SQL function: gopgext writes the C glue, the install script and the control file.

Experimentalgopgext is experimental. Don’t use it in production: a bug in the generated code or the Go runtime runs inside the server, where it can crash it or corrupt data, and the API and generated SQL may change without notice.

Just Go

A project is plain Go files. The standard library works: fmt, regexp, encoding/json, crypto/*, maps, generics, iterators, defer/recover.

Types map to SQL

Strings, numbers, arrays, NULLs, sets, rows, timestamps, UUIDs and JSON map to SQL types. Define your own data types and composite types in Go.

Queries and errors

Run SQL through SPI, return errors with SQLSTATE codes, log, read settings and stay responsive to query cancellation.

Beyond functions

Write triggers, aggregates, GiST, GIN, SP-GiST and BRIN operator classes, index access methods, foreign data wrappers and query hooks.

Proven on contrib

Ports of PostgreSQL’s contrib modules (pgcrypto, hstore, pg_stat_statements, cube, …) pass upstream’s regression tests.

Safe coexistence

Several Go extensions load in one backend. PostgreSQL errors never unwind through Go frames, and results are copied into PostgreSQL memory.

Hello, world#

package main

import (
	"strings"

	"gopgext/pg"
)

// Hello returns a greeting for name.
//
//gopgext:function immutable parallel=safe
func Hello(name string) string {
	return "Hello, " + name + "!"
}

// Shout upper-cases s. An empty string raises an error.
//
//gopgext:function immutable parallel=safe
func Shout(s string) (string, error) {
	if s == "" {
		return "", pg.Errorf(pg.CodeInvalidParameterValue, "nothing to shout")
	}
	return strings.ToUpper(s) + "!", nil
}

func main() {} // runs once per backend, when PostgreSQL loads the library

gopgext init hello       # creates hello/go.mod and hello/main.go
gopgext install hello    # builds hello.so, hello.control, hello--1.0.sql and installs them
psql -c 'CREATE EXTENSION hello' -c "SELECT hello('world')"
#     hello
# ---------------
#  Hello, world!

The tutorial walks through it step by step.

A sibling project#

gopgext uses the same approach as gokm, which builds Linux kernel modules from Go: a custom TinyGo target and runtime layer for the host, a C runtime compiled by the host’s own build system (PGXS here, kbuild there), and generated glue.

Announced at alpo.ge/remark.pdf on 20 November 2026.

Summary

The published Lean source compiles without errors, the five headline theorems depend only on the three standard axioms, every module has been replayed through the Lean kernel, two independently written kernels, nanoda and con-leche, accept the full exported proof, and lean4lean accepts every compiled module. What was verified

Five theorems, proved in the submission's Main.lean. Their statements are below exactly as they appear in the challenge file, which imports only Mathlib. All the mathematical notions in them (riemannZeta, DirichletCharacter, DirichletCharacter.LFunction, IsPrimitive) are Mathlib's.

1. The Riemann Hypothesis, using Mathlib's own definition (Mathlib/NumberTheory/LSeries/RiemannZeta.lean): every zero of ζ other than the trivial zeros −2, −4, −6, … has real part 1/2. The condition s ≠ 1 is there because Mathlib assigns ζ a conventional value at its pole.

def RiemannHypothesis : Prop :=
  ∀ (s : ℂ) (_ : riemannZeta s = 0) (_ : ¬∃ n : ℕ, s = -2 * (n + 1)) (_ : s ≠ 1), s.re = 1 / 2

theorem riemannHypothesis : RiemannHypothesis

2. The same statement written out in the submission's own words. Lean accepts the two as equal by definition.

theorem riemannZeta_eq_zero_re :
  ∀ s : ℂ, riemannZeta s = 0 → (¬∃ n : ℕ, s = -2 * ((n : ℂ) + 1)) → s ≠ 1 → s.re = 1 / 2

3. No zeros to the right of the critical line, for every Dirichlet L-function. For every modulus N ≥ 1 and every Dirichlet character χ modulo N, primitive or not, L(χ, s) ≠ 0 whenever Re s > 1/2. The one excluded case is the trivial character at s = 1, where the L-function has its pole.

theorem LFunction_ne_zero_of_half_lt_re :
  ∀ (N : ℕ) [NeZero N] (χ : DirichletCharacter ℂ N) (s : ℂ),
    1 / 2 < s.re → (χ ≠ 1 ∨ s ≠ 1) → DirichletCharacter.LFunction χ s ≠ 0

4. Zeros in the critical strip lie on the critical line, for every Dirichlet L-function.

theorem LFunction_eq_zero_re :
  ∀ (N : ℕ) [NeZero N] (χ : DirichletCharacter ℂ N) (s : ℂ),
    0 < s.re → s.re < 1 → DirichletCharacter.LFunction χ s = 0 → s.re = 1 / 2

5. The same for primitive characters, the form in which the Generalized Riemann Hypothesis for Dirichlet L-functions is usually stated.

theorem LFunction_eq_zero_re_of_isPrimitive :
  ∀ (N : ℕ) [NeZero N] (χ : DirichletCharacter ℂ N), χ.IsPrimitive →
    ∀ s : ℂ, 0 < s.re → s.re < 1 → DirichletCharacter.LFunction χ s = 0 → s.re = 1 / 2

Scope. "GRH" here means Dirichlet L-functions: all moduli and all characters. Dedekind zeta functions, Hecke L-functions and automorphic L-functions in general are not among the statements that were checked.

Arithmetic consequences

As a check that does not depend on Mathlib's definition of the zeta function, the proof was combined with kimihiro64/Robin1984 (commit acab1a3), an independent formalization of Robin's and Lagarias's criteria on the same Lean and Mathlib versions. Importing both gives two theorems about the divisor sum, with no hypotheses and no mention of zeta (ArithSolution.lean; statements alone in ArithChallenge.lean, which imports only Mathlib):

theorem robin_inequality :
    ∀ n : ℕ, 5040 < n →
      ((ArithmeticFunction.sigma 1 n : ℕ) : ℝ) <
        Real.exp Real.eulerMascheroniConstant * (n : ℝ) * Real.log (Real.log (n : ℝ))

theorem lagarias_inequality :
    ∀ n : ℕ, 0 < n →
      ((ArithmeticFunction.sigma 1 n : ℕ) : ℝ) ≤
        (harmonic n : ℝ) + Real.exp (harmonic n : ℝ) * Real.log (harmonic n : ℝ)

Check it yourself
